title: DHS Makes End of 540-Day Work Permit Extension Permanent in Final Rule
excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security's final rule, effective on Federal Register publication on October 14, means most EAD renewals filed on or after October 30, 2025 no longer extend work authorization while they are pending — a direct hit for H-4 spouses and asylum applicants.
body:
• DHS has issued a final rule making permanent the end of the automatic 540-day extension of employment authorization documents (EADs) for most renewals.
  • The rule was released for public inspection on October 13, is scheduled for Federal Register publication on October 14, 2026, and takes effect on publication.
  • It applies to most renewals filed on or after October 30, 2025; timely renewals filed before that date may still keep up to 540 days of continued authorization.
  • If you hold an H-4, asylum or adjustment-of-status EAD: file your renewal at the earliest date allowed — 180 days before expiry — because a pending case no longer lets you keep working after the card expires.

The Department of Homeland Security has finalised a rule ending the automatic extension of work authorization for most people renewing an employment authorization document (EAD), according to Bloomberg Law reporting carried by Bloomberg Tax and Mint. The final rule, released for public inspection on October 13, makes permanent an interim final rule issued on October 30, 2025.

Under the system being ended, eligible applicants who filed a timely renewal before their card expired could generally keep working for up to 540 days while US Citizenship and Immigration Services processed the case. For most renewals filed on or after October 30, 2025, a pending application will no longer extend work authorization past the card's printed expiration date.

Who is affected

The rule reaches several EAD categories, including H-4 spouses of H-1B workers (category c)(26), asylum applicants (c)(8), and people with pending adjustment-of-status applications (c)(9), among others listed in the earlier interim rule. Narrow exceptions remain for extensions provided by statute or by Federal Register notice, such as certain TPS-based EADs, and for STEM OPT. DHS estimates that 20,000 to 33,000 EADs could lapse over the 18 months beginning in May 2027, according to VisaVerge's summary of the rule.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=BPUhAW4jsXE

DHS said the change would allow officials to vet applicants more frequently. The 540-day extension, first made permanent in January 2025, had been designed to stop workers being pushed out of jobs purely because of USCIS processing delays.

The backlog the extension was built for has not gone away

By June 30, 2026, more than 432,000 work permit renewal applications had been pending at USCIS for six months, including more than 91,000 pending for over 18 months, according to figures cited by Bloomberg Law. Foreign workers cannot file a renewal more than 180 days before their card expires, which leaves no buffer when processing runs past six months.

During the comment period, H-4 EAD holders — women form the majority — warned that H-4 processing times frequently exceed the 180-day filing window, risking unavoidable work gaps, lost health insurance and possible eviction. A group of H-4 visa holders sued in January, arguing the change violated the Administrative Procedure Act; in September a California judge blocked the interim final rule from applying to those plaintiffs, finding the agency had not met procedural requirements or accounted for their reliance on the previous policy.

What this means for you

If your EAD expires in the next year, the practical rules have changed: file on day 180 before expiry, keep the receipt notice with your employer, and talk to your employer's HR before the card expires, because working past the printed date without an approved renewal is now unauthorised employment for most categories. The rule is separate from, but lands alongside, DHS's proposal to end deference to prior H-1B and L-1 approvals, which we reported in DHS Proposes Ending Deference to Prior H-1B and L-1 Petition Approvals. Renewal categories and filing windows are set out on the rule summary; for case-specific advice, an immigration attorney remains the right call.

What to watch

The final rule takes effect on publication in the Federal Register on October 14. Litigation over the interim rule is already in the courts, and further challenges to the final rule are likely; any injunction would be reported here as it lands.
